title: Functions, Memory and the Call Stack
oneLiner: What happens in memory when one function calls another, why a copied list can change "by itself", and how a function can call itself (recursion).
keyTakeaway: Each function call gets a stack frame holding its parameters and local variables; frames pile up on the call stack as calls nest and are thrown away as they return. Small values such as numbers are copied when assigned, but objects such as lists live elsewhere (the heap) and variables hold references to them, so two names can share one list. Recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case it can answer directly.
explanation:
A function is a named, reusable piece of code: you call it with some inputs (arguments, which arrive as its parameters), it runs, and it returns a result to whoever called it. The interesting part is the bookkeeping. When main calls area, and area calls multiply, the program has to remember where it was in each one and what its local variables were, so that when multiply returns, area carries on exactly where it left off.

It does that with the call stack. Every call pushes a stack frame on top: a small block of memory with that call's parameters, its local variables and the place to return to. Only the top frame is running; the ones below are paused, waiting. When a function returns, its frame is popped off and its local variables disappear, which is why a local variable can't be used after its function ends. It's called a stack because, like a stack of plates, the last frame added is the first one removed.

Not everything fits in a frame. Objects that can outlive a call, such as lists, dictionaries and class instances, live in a separate area called the heap, and a variable holds a reference to the object (in effect, its address) rather than the object itself. So b = a copies a number, but ys = xs copies only the reference: both names now point at one list, and appending through ys changes what xs sees too. This surprises almost everyone once. Stack vs Heap and Garbage Collection, in Concurrency & Memory, goes deeper.

Recursion is a function that calls itself. It works because each call gets its own frame with its own copy of the parameters, so factorial(3) can call factorial(2) without the two interfering. Every recursive function needs a base case, an input small enough to answer directly (factorial(1) = 1), and a recursive case that moves toward it. Forget the base case and the frames keep piling up until the memory reserved for the stack runs out: a stack overflow.
